explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. God says Jerusalem is the daughter of her mother, who "…despised her husband and children." (Ezekiel 16:45) That's the family resemblance the proverb points to. I think this one is heavy, because it's about turning away from the people closest to you.

Home and fields don't show up in this verse, friend. God says the mother "…despised her husband and children." (Ezekiel 16:45) The proverb is about family, and it's about a people who turned away from the ones closest to them. Easy one to mix up when you're guessing at what a mother might despise.

Good guess if you're thinking of the idols earlier in the message, but this verse says something different. The mother "…despised her husband and children." (Ezekiel 16:45) The same goes for Jerusalem's sisters. So the family trait here is turning away from the people who should have been loved.

Yes, baker! God says, "Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) Samaria is the older sister here, and she had her daughters with her. Jerusalem's family is bigger than just the one sister.

God doesn't name Damascus here, friend. He says Jerusalem's older sister "…was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) It's a fair guess when you're picturing a northern neighbor. The verse just gives a different name.

The verse names someone else, friend: "Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north…" (Ezekiel 16:46) Samaria is the one God puts in the family. Tyre isn't in this lineup at all.

That's it, baker. God says, "…your younger sister was Sodom, who lived with her daughters to your south." (Ezekiel 16:46) So Jerusalem has an older sister to the north and a younger one to the south. She's sitting right in the middle of the family photo.

Bethel isn't the sister here, friend. God says, "…your younger sister was Sodom, who lived with her daughters to your south." (Ezekiel 16:46) Sodom is the name He gives. Bethel doesn't show up in this verse.

Babylon isn't the sister here, friend. In this verse God names the younger sister as Sodom, who "…lived with her daughters to your south." (Ezekiel 16:46) Babylon isn't part of this family. The sisters are Samaria and Sodom.

explanations.answer: She became more depraved than they were
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. God says she walked in their ways and practiced their abominations, "…but soon you were more depraved than they were." (Ezekiel 16:47) She didn't just follow her sisters. She went further than they did. I think this verse is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: She turned and warned them to stop
explanations.explanation: That's not what God says, friend. Jerusalem "…walked in their ways and practiced their abominations…" and "…soon you were more depraved than they were." (Ezekiel 16:47) The verse doesn't say she warned them. It says she walked in their ways and then went further.

explanations.answer: She stayed just as bad as they were
explanations.explanation: Close, but the verse goes further than that. God says, "…soon you were more depraved than they were." (Ezekiel 16:47) So she didn't just match her sisters. She topped them, and that's what makes this verse so heavy.

True, baker. God says Sodom and her daughters "…did not help the poor and needy." (Ezekiel 16:49) They were arrogant, overfed and complacent, and that's the iniquity God names. Notice that He lists it plainly, with no extra commentary needed.

This one is actually true. God's list of Sodom's iniquity ends with this: they "…did not help the poor and needy." (Ezekiel 16:49) It sits right next to being arrogant, overfed and complacent. The text says it outright, so the statement holds.
Yes, baker. God says her abominations "…have made your sisters appear righteous." (Ezekiel 16:51) That's how far Jerusalem went. She made Samaria and Sodom look better just by standing next to them.

I get why you went there, since the whole passage is heavy. But the verse says her abominations "…have made your sisters appear righteous." (Ezekiel 16:51) The sisters weren't made to look worse. Jerusalem went so far that they looked better by comparison.

Foolish sounds like a fair word here, but it's not the one God uses. He says her abominations "…have made your sisters appear righteous." (Ezekiel 16:51) It's about how she stacks up next to them. Her sins were so many that her sisters looked good in comparison.

I see the logic, but God says the opposite. "So now you must bear your disgrace, since you have brought justification for your sisters." (Ezekiel 16:52) Her sisters appearing more righteous doesn't get her off the hook. It's the very reason she has to bear it.

False is right, baker. God says, "So you too must bear your shame and disgrace, since you have made your sisters appear righteous." (Ezekiel 16:52) Her sisters looking better doesn't lift anything off her. Jerusalem has to carry it herself.

Not quite, friend. God says, "…I will restore Sodom and her daughters from captivity, as well as Samaria and her daughters. And I will restore you along with them." (Ezekiel 16:53) Jerusalem is in on it too. Nobody gets left out of that sentence.

False is right, baker. God says He will restore Sodom and Samaria, and then adds, "And I will restore you along with them." (Ezekiel 16:53) Jerusalem is right there with her sisters. After all that heavy talk, that's quite the turn.

That's it, baker. God says, "So you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them." (Ezekiel 16:54) The word is ashamed, and it comes right after the promise to restore. I think that shows she'll see her past plainly.

Proud isn't the word here, friend. God says, "…you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them." (Ezekiel 16:54) So the feeling the verse names is shame. It doesn't name pride.

Glad doesn't fit this verse. God says, "…you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them." (Ezekiel 16:54) The word He uses is ashamed. Gladness isn't in the picture for what she did.

Right, baker. God asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) That was before her own wickedness was uncovered. I think this one stings a little.

That's not what God says, friend. He asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) Scorn is the word. Rescue isn't what the verse describes.

A visit sounds nice, but that's not the picture. God asks, "Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride…" (Ezekiel 16:56) So she looked down on Sodom. Scorn is the word the verse uses.

explanations.answer: The oath by breaking the covenant
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "I will deal with you according to your deeds, since you have despised the oath by breaking the covenant." (Ezekiel 16:59) The oath and the covenant go together here. She broke what she had sworn to keep.

explanations.answer: The law by ignoring the priests
explanations.explanation: The priests don't come up in this verse, friend. God says she "…despised the oath by breaking the covenant." (Ezekiel 16:59) That's the thing He names. The verse keeps its eye on the oath and the covenant.

That's a heavy guess, and the verse doesn't say it. God says she "…despised the oath by breaking the covenant." (Ezekiel 16:59) Prophets and stones aren't mentioned here. The oath and the covenant are the focus.

True, baker, and what a turn that is. God says, "…I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth…" (Ezekiel 16:60) She broke the covenant, and He still says He will remember it. That one gets me every time.

I see why you'd think that after the covenant got broken. But God says, "But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth…" (Ezekiel 16:60) He says it Himself, so the statement is true. That little word "But" changes everything.
Yes, baker! God says, "…I will establish an everlasting covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:60) Everlasting means it doesn't run out. After a broken covenant, that's a big promise to hear.

Temporary would be a letdown, friend, and it's not what God says. He says, "…I will establish an everlasting covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:60) Everlasting is the word. It's the opposite of something with an expiration date.
The verse doesn't attach any conditions, friend. God says, "…I will establish an everlasting covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:60) He calls it everlasting, and that's the word to hold on to.

True, baker. God says, "I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:61) That's in the same verse where Jerusalem remembers her ways and is ashamed when she receives her older and younger sisters. The family gets bigger.

This one is true, friend. God says, "I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you." (Ezekiel 16:61) So the sisters really are given to her that way. It's the reason behind it that He adds a note about.

That's right, baker. God says, "So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 16:62) The knowing is about who He is. It's a good place for this long message to land.

Earning doesn't show up in this verse, friend. God says, "…I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 16:62) What she'll know is about Him. It's not about what she did.

Her sisters aren't what she'll know, friend. God says, "…you will know that I am the LORD…" (Ezekiel 16:62) That's what she'll know when He establishes His covenant. The verse puts the focus on who He is.

True, baker. God says that when He makes atonement for all she has done, she will "…never again open your mouth because of your disgrace…" (Ezekiel 16:63) That's the last line of the message. The one who makes atonement is God Himself.

This one is true, friend. God says that when He makes atonement, she will remember and be ashamed and "…never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD." (Ezekiel 16:63) It's right there in the very last verse. Good news is still waiting around the heavy parts.
